strengths: The paper addresses a concrete bottleneck in language-based 3D perception: autoregressive SceneScript-style layout generation is slow, and the proposed multi-token decoding pipeline gives a clear practical speed/accuracy tradeoff.

The method is technically coherent: multi-token prediction is combined with reliability filtering, with two variants that have distinct deployment profiles: SSD for higher accepted-token throughput and CGD for on-the-fly confidence-based stopping.

The experiments show consistent gains over the immediate baseline. On ASE, Fast SceneScript with SSD at n=10 reports similar mean F1 to SceneScript while reducing latency from 382 ms to 75 ms; on Structured3D it improves mean F1 over SceneScript while reducing latency from 1176 ms to 211-269 ms depending on decoding.

The ablations are useful and targeted. They isolate the impact of numerical-token tolerance, confidence-guided decoding versus softmax/product thresholding, and the proposed head-sharing parameter-efficient mechanism.

The parameter-efficiency contribution is practically meaningful: the proposed shared-head design keeps decoder parameters close to the base SceneScript model, while naive MTP substantially increases parameters and hurts accuracy.
weaknesses: The originality is moderate rather than high. The main ingredients, multi-token prediction, speculative/self-verification, and confidence scoring, are adapted from language-model inference; the vision-specific novelty is mainly their application and tuning for structured 3D layout tokens.

The scope of evidence is narrower than some of the paper's broader claims. The method is positioned as a general acceleration strategy for language-based perception, but experiments are only on 3D scene layout estimation, not object detection, part reconstruction, or other structured perception tasks.

Latency reporting is not fully transparent. The paper reports decoder latency and decoder parameter counts, but does not clearly give end-to-end runtime including the 3D encoder, preprocessing, memory cost, batching effects, or hardware utilization. This matters because the practical speedup may be smaller in a full pipeline.

The SSD accounting is somewhat confusing: SSD requires an additional verification pass, yet the paper emphasizes accepted tokens per decoder inference. More explicit reporting of total decoder calls per generated sequence and sequence lengths would make the claimed 9-token-per-step acceleration easier to verify.

Some CGD training details are under-specified. The confidence targets are defined through agreement between first-head and future-head outputs, but the manuscript does not fully clarify whether these are argmax predictions under teacher forcing, sampled predictions, or ground-truth-aligned outputs, nor how the inference threshold epsilon is selected.

The evaluation lacks statistical robustness: no confidence intervals, repeated training runs, or significance analysis are provided, even though some accuracy differences between SceneScript and Fast SceneScript are small on ASE.

Reproducibility is incomplete from the manuscript alone. Several details needed to reproduce results are missing or deferred, such as exact tokenization/quantization conventions, decoding thresholds for CGD, full learning-rate schedule, sequence length statistics, and the supplementary results for larger n.

The comparison to RoomFormer is useful but limited. Fast SceneScript is more accurate but substantially slower on Structured3D, and the argument that it is more general is not experimentally demonstrated in this paper.

strengths: The paper targets a concrete bottleneck in language-based 3D layout estimation: autoregressive decoding latency in SceneScript-style structured output models. This is a relevant practical problem, and the reported latency reductions are substantial on the evaluated benchmarks.

The empirical tables are reasonably focused: they compare vanilla SceneScript, naive MTP variants, and the proposed SSD/CGD filtering variants across ASE and Structured3D. The results show that naive MTP harms F1 substantially, while token filtering largely recovers baseline accuracy with much lower latency.

The parameter-sharing mechanism is simple but useful: the reported decoder parameter count is much lower than naive multi-head MTP, and the ablation suggests sharing does not materially hurt accuracy.
The paper includes ablations for numerical-token tolerance, scoring-based alternatives, and head sharing, which helps isolate the proposed components.
weaknesses: The core novelty is limited. The method is largely an application of known multi-token prediction and speculative/scoring-based decoding ideas to SceneScript, with a straightforward head-sharing design. The paper does not convincingly establish a broader computer vision contribution beyond adapting existing LLM acceleration techniques to one structured 3D layout pipeline.

The evaluation scope is narrow relative to the claims. Although the motivation repeatedly frames the method as useful for language-based perception generalists and other 3D tasks, experiments cover only 3D scene layout estimation on ASE and Structured3D. There is no evidence on 3D object detection, part reconstruction, or other structured perception tasks where token dependencies and error tolerance may differ.

The main speed claims are under-specified. The paper reports latency but does not sufficiently describe the measurement protocol, hardware, batch size, whether encoder time is included, decoding implementation details, or variance. Since the contribution is primarily efficiency, this missing information materially weakens the evidence.

Some comparisons are not fully convincing. The strongest baseline is a naive SceneScript+MTP model that predictably loses accuracy without filtering; more competitive adapted baselines for speculative decoding, confidence calibration, or optimized autoregressive decoding are not explored. The comparison to RoomFormer also uses decoder parameters for language models, which is not a fully comparable measure of total model cost.

The technical description of confidence-guided decoding is unclear in important places. The construction of confidence labels depends on comparing additional-head predictions to first-head predictions, but the manuscript does not clearly specify whether these are argmax predictions, teacher-forced predictions, sampled outputs, or how this is handled during training. The confidence threshold epsilon is also not reported in the main text.

Reproducibility is incomplete. Several implementation details needed to reproduce the method are missing or vague, including projection block dimensions, tokenization/discretization details for numerical coordinates, the units and scale of tau, threshold choices for CGD, exact latency setup, learning-rate schedule milestones, and whether all baselines were tuned comparably.

The accuracy gains over the retrained SceneScript baseline are small or nonexistent on ASE: Fast SceneScript is slightly below the retrained baseline mean F1 in Table 1 while being much faster. That is still useful, but the wording sometimes overstates the accuracy contribution by emphasizing improvements over weak naive MTP variants.

The paper does not provide uncertainty estimates, multiple training seeds, or statistical analysis. Given that some reported differences are on the order of 0.001 to 0.005 F1, it is hard to know which accuracy differences are meaningful.

The qualitative figures are not very diagnostic. They visually suggest that Fast SceneScript is better than naive MTP, but they do not expose common failure modes, cases where filtering stops too early, or errors introduced by numerical tolerance.

Overall, the paper has a practical idea and promising numbers, but the limited originality, narrow validation, and insufficiently specified efficiency/reproducibility details make the current submission fall below the acceptance bar for CVPR.

strengths: The paper addresses a clear bottleneck in language-based 3D layout estimation: autoregressive structured-token decoding is slow, and the proposed Fast SceneScript substantially improves latency while maintaining essentially the same F1 as the NTP SceneScript baseline.

The technical approach is sensible and well matched to the task. Multi-token prediction exploits the deterministic structure of layout token sequences, while SSD/CGD token filtering directly targets the main failure mode of naive MTP: inaccurate future tokens.

The empirical results are strong on the paper's stated target. On ASE, Fast SceneScript reaches about 5x lower decoding latency than SceneScript with nearly identical mean F1, and on Structured3D it improves mean F1 while reducing latency by more than 4-5x depending on the decoding mode.

The ablations are useful: the paper isolates naive MTP degradation, the numerical-token tolerance in SSD, CGD versus softmax/product thresholding, and the parameter-sharing mechanism. These experiments support the main design choices rather than only reporting final numbers.

The parameter-efficient head-sharing design is practically valuable. It reduces the large parameter overhead of naive MTP while preserving accuracy, making the method more attractive than simply adding many future-token heads.
The manuscript is generally clear, with helpful diagrams and tables that make the inference procedure, filtering strategies, and accuracy/speed tradeoffs easy to follow.
weaknesses: The novelty is incremental rather than fundamental: MTP, speculative decoding, confidence scoring, and shared heads are all adapted from existing language-model inference ideas. The main contribution is a well-executed transfer to structured 3D layout generation, not a broadly new decoding principle.

The evaluation scope is narrower than some of the claims. The method is motivated as useful for language-based perception generalists and potentially other 3D perception tasks, but experiments only cover 3D layout estimation with SceneScript-style outputs. No evidence is provided for object detection, part reconstruction, or other structured perception tasks.

Latency reporting is not fully characterized. The tables report decoding time on an RTX 2080 Ti, but do not clearly discuss end-to-end runtime including the 3D encoder, variance across scenes, batching conditions, sequence length distributions, or memory use. This makes the practical speedup harder to interpret beyond the reported setup.

Several important reproducibility details are under-specified. The CGD confidence threshold epsilon is not stated in the main text, threshold selection for competing scoring methods is only briefly described, and the multi-step learning-rate schedule details are missing. Code availability is also not discussed in the manuscript.

The comparison to RoomFormer is somewhat uneven. The paper correctly notes that RoomFormer is task-specific, but Fast SceneScript is still much slower in latency; the argument for generality remains mostly conceptual because only layout estimation is evaluated.

The accuracy gains over the retrained SceneScript baseline are small on ASE, where Fast SceneScript is mainly a speed/parameter contribution. This is still valuable, but the paper should avoid framing the method as broadly more accurate except where Structured3D results support that claim.

The numerical-token tolerance in SSD is plausible, but its effect on geometric validity is not deeply analyzed. Accepting near-matching coordinate tokens may preserve F1 while still changing structural consistency, and the paper does not report validity/error modes of the generated layouts.

The paper relies heavily on a supplementary material for some sensitivity analysis, such as larger n values and additional details, but the main manuscript provides limited evidence about robustness to hyperparameters and thresholds.

strengths: The paper addresses a concrete bottleneck in language-based 3D perception: autoregressive SceneScript-style decoding is slow, and the proposed multi-token prediction pipeline gives large reported decoding speedups while largely preserving accuracy.
weaknesses: The technical novelty is moderate. The core ingredients, multi-token prediction, self-speculative decoding, confidence/scoring-based filtering, and head sharing, are adaptations of existing LLM acceleration ideas rather than fundamentally new modeling concepts.

strengths: The paper addresses a real bottleneck in language-based 3D perception: autoregressive decoding latency. The reported speedups over SceneScript are large, e.g. 382 ms to 75-92 ms on ASE layout and 535 ms to 104-108 ms on ASE object detection.

The method is technically plausible and well aligned with the structure of the output space. Multi-token prediction, self-speculative verification, and confidence-guided filtering are reasonable mechanisms for semi-deterministic scene-token sequences.

The evaluation covers multiple settings: synthetic layout estimation on ASE and Structured3D, real-world SceneCAD, and object detection on ASE/SceneCAD. The ablations isolate token filtering, numerical-token tolerance, confidence thresholds, and parameter sharing.

The parameter-sharing mechanism is useful: it substantially reduces decoder parameters relative to naive MTP while maintaining much of the accuracy, which is a practical contribution for this class of models.
weaknesses: The originality is limited. The main ideas are adaptations of existing multi-token prediction, speculative decoding, confidence/threshold filtering, and head sharing to SceneScript-style outputs. The paper does not make a strong case that the algorithmic contribution is deep beyond this application-specific packaging.

Several headline claims are overstated. The paper repeatedly says accuracy is preserved, but on ASE layout the best fast variants are slightly below the retrained SceneScript baseline on test mean F1 (e.g. 0.913 or 0.912 vs 0.915), and SceneCAD layout CGD is also lower than SceneScript. These drops are small, but the text should not present the result as uniformly uncompromised accuracy.

The usefulness is narrower than the framing suggests. On Structured3D, RoomFormer is still much faster than Fast SceneScript for layout estimation (54 ms vs 211-269 ms), so the method is mainly attractive when one specifically wants a SceneScript-like general language interface rather than fastest task-specific perception.

The object detection evaluation is not fully convincing. ASE object boxes are generated using TR3D predictions on reconstructed point clouds rather than public ground truth annotations, so the detection benchmark partly evaluates agreement with a generated teacher. This weakens the evidence for real detection quality.

The latency accounting is not sufficiently transparent. The paper reports decoder latency and decoder parameters, but the end-to-end cost including the 3D encoder and any implementation details for batching/cache reuse is not clearly characterized. Since the contribution is primarily efficiency, fuller profiling is important.

The confidence-guided decoding supervision is conceptually questionable: confidence labels are based on agreement with the first head rather than correctness against ground truth. The supplementary ablation compares a GT variant, but the explanation remains thin, and it is unclear whether the learned confidence estimates reliability or merely internal consistency.

The evaluation is centered almost entirely on SceneScript-derived models. There is little comparison to alternative acceleration strategies, optimized autoregressive decoding implementations, distillation, non-autoregressive structured prediction, or other 3D perception generalists beyond limited RoomFormer/SceneScript baselines.

Reproducibility is only moderate. Some implementation details are given, but important pieces such as exact splits, generated ASE detection labels, threshold selection protocol, hardware/runtime setup, and code availability are not sufficiently specified for easy independent verification.

The paper contains presentation issues that reduce confidence: some claims are numerically selective, several percentage improvements are framed relative to weak naive MTP baselines rather than the strongest baseline, and there are grammar/wording problems. These are not fatal alone, but they contribute to an impression of overclaiming.

strengths: The paper addresses a concrete bottleneck in language-based 3D scene understanding: autoregressive decoding latency. Applying multi-token prediction to structured 3D scene languages is well motivated, and the paper clearly explains why this setting is more amenable to multi-token decoding than open-ended natural language generation.

The empirical speedups are substantial while preserving accuracy. On ASE layout estimation, Fast SceneScript reduces latency from 382 ms to 75-92 ms with nearly unchanged mean F1, and on ASE object detection it reduces latency from 535 ms to about 104-108 ms with slightly higher F1. Similar trends are reported on Structured3D and SceneCAD.

The paper includes useful ablations separating plain MTP, SSD filtering, CGD filtering, numerical-token tolerance, softmax/product-threshold baselines, and head sharing. These make the central claims more credible, especially the claim that naive MTP is fast but inaccurate and that filtering recovers accuracy.

The parameter-efficient head-sharing mechanism is practically valuable: it avoids the large parameter growth of naive MTP and is shown to retain accuracy. The comparison with and without sharing is convincing enough for the claimed efficiency benefit.

The manuscript is generally clear, with understandable diagrams and tables. The supplement adds helpful details on training, thresholds, accepted-token distributions, longer baseline training, and failure cases.
weaknesses: The core algorithmic novelty is moderate. The paper mainly adapts known multi-token prediction, speculative decoding, confidence scoring, and head sharing ideas to SceneScript-style structured outputs. This adaptation is useful, but the conceptual leap is not very large.

Evaluation is mostly within the SceneScript family. Comparisons to specialized 3D layout methods are limited, and object detection is compared only against SceneScript variants rather than standard 3D detectors. This makes it harder to assess broader usefulness beyond accelerating one class of language-based models.

The object detection setup on ASE uses TR3D-generated pseudo boxes from dense ground-truth depth because annotations are unavailable. This weakens the evidential value of the object detection results as a benchmark for real detection quality, even if it is adequate for testing decoding speed and consistency.

Latency is reported as decoding time on a single RTX 2080 Ti, with limited detail about end-to-end timing, encoder cost, batching, implementation optimizations, and variance. Since the main contribution is efficiency, more complete runtime characterization would strengthen the claim.

The real-world SceneCAD layout results are modest: Fast SceneScript matches or slightly underperforms SceneScript in layout F1 while improving latency. This supports efficiency but makes the accuracy-preservation claim less uniformly strong across settings.

Reproducibility is only partially addressed. The supplement gives training settings and split filenames, but the paper does not clearly state code/model release plans or provide enough detail to regenerate pseudo labels and all data preprocessing choices independently.
